abstract: ABSTRACT Rationale In mass spectrometry measurements, mass shifts may be inadvertently introduced due to instrumental drift and calibration inaccuracies, potentially compromising the accuracy of subsequent data analysis. This work presents a novel, label‐free algorithm to improve relative mass alignment between mass spectra. The warping function is modeled as a natural cubic spline, a suitable model for gradual, nonlinear mass shifts. Methods The algorithm is validated on a dataset generated from human glioblastoma multiforme samples using matrix‐assisted laser desorption/ionization time‐of‐flight mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI‐TOF MSI) and rapid evaporative ionization mass spectrometry (REIMS), and public datasets generated from MALDI‐TOF and desorption electrospray ionization (DESI) Orbitrap instruments. Results The algorithm considerably reduces the mass dispersion of the dataset and improves the similarity to a reference mass spectrum for MALDI‐TOF, REIMS and DESI‐Orbitrap data. It is demonstrated that the proposed method reliably corrects for severe mass shifts. The algorithm is competitive in speed and mass dispersion reduction compared to MSIWarp, a common method to correct for mass misalignment. Conclusions This paper presents a novel algorithm to reduce relative mass misalignment for mass spectrometry, validated on an extensive dataset. Thanks to the use of profile data, the peak shapes contribute to the computation of the warping function, and the warping function is approximated in a robust manner. An open‐source Python implementation of the proposed methodology will be made accessible on GitHub: https://github.com/VanhemelThomas/psalign .

Methods
The goal of the alignment procedure is to compute a warping function that maximizes a similarity metric between a reference spectrum and a moving spectrum. This procedure is applied to all spectra to align them to a common reference mass spectrum. The reference spectrum used is the average mass spectrum after total ion current (TIC) normalization [
1
], unless explicitly indicated otherwise. In this text, this mass spectrum is referred to as the
average spectrum
. This spectrum usually contains shared information across pixels and a consistent biological signal. Evidently, the efficacy of data‐driven mass alignment depends on the availability of sufficient shared information between the reference and moving spectrum. The methodology for relative mass alignment presented in this paper consists of four steps. First, the mass spectrum is divided into segments of equal size and the maximum peak within that segment is identified. Second, a local window around that peak is compared with the reference spectrum; the shift that maximizes the similarity estimates the local mass shift. Third, a warping function is calculated based on the local mass shifts after an optional outlier detection step. Fourth, the parameters of the warping function are optimized to maximize a similarity metric. Figure
2
gives an overview of the proposed algorithm.

(A) The mass spectrum is divided into segments of equal size and a window around the largest peak is taken and a slightly larger window is extracted from the reference mass spectrum. (B) The mass spectrum window slides over the reference spectrum window in order to identify the optimal local mass shift. The similarity score across the shifts is visualized and the optimal local mass shift is highlighted. (C) An optional outlier detection procedure is applied to the detected local mass shifts or knots and outliers are removed. (D) The warping function is computed based on the knots and the knots are adjusted to maximize a similarity metric.

2.2
Obtaining a Robust Initial Estimate
Given the abundance of peaks present in mass spectrometry, it is expected that the optimization problem has numerous suboptimal minimizers. Consequently, a global optimization algorithm would be advantageous; however, given the need to repeat the procedure for each pixel of a MS image, the associated computation time would rapidly become excessive. Hence, an alternative strategy is explored that uses a gradient‐based algorithm to improve a good initial estimate.
In order to obtain a good initial estimate for the warping function,
q
is divided into segments, and the highest peak is found per segment (Figure
2A
). Then, a section containing the largest peak is extracted and matched to the reference spectrum, meaning that the local shift is found that maximizes the dot product between the reference spectrum and the section containing the largest peak (see Figure
2B
). The use of the dot product facilitates the identification of corresponding peaks because the peak shape provides additional information for the determination of the mass shift, making the proposed method more robust. This information would be absent if the mass spectrum were peak‐picked or centroided. Additionally, this operation, in combination with the use of the cosine similarity, requires that the moving and reference spectrum are sampled at identical m/z values. In the case of profile data, the m/z array of the moving spectrum can be interpolated to the m/z array of the reference spectrum. For sparse centroided data, a shared m/z array can be constructed based on all the measured m/z values in subsequent measurements. The initial m/z array is chosen as the array of the measurement with the largest number of m/z bins. The m/z values are then added to the shared m/z array iteratively, provided that the distance from the m/z value to the shared m/z array is greater than the expected distance between m/z values in a sample across the measurements. Subsequently, the intensity measurements are interpolated from the measured m/z array to the shared m/z array. The m/z values that correspond to the most prominent peaks in the average spectrum can be retained to limit memory requirements.
An optional outlier detection approach is implemented to remove erroneous matches should they occur (see Figure
2C
). A sliding window of size five is applied to consecutive detected mass shifts and their associated m/z values. Within each window, the mass shift trend is approximately linear, allowing the reliable detection of outliers using a relatively small window size. The detection of outliers is akin to the RANSAC [
14
] algorithm: (i) select two mass shifts and their associated m/z values from the window and fit a linear model; (ii) detect mass shifts of the window, which are consistent with the linear model, and (iii) repeat steps (i)–(ii) for all possible choices of two mass shifts out of the window of five and select the model, which maximizes the number of mass shifts consistent with the model. If there are multiple solutions, select the model with the smallest error on the consistent set of mass shifts. A minimum of three points per window is needed to detect a single outlier, as two points define the local linear fit and a third provides the redundancy needed to evaluate deviations. Extending the window to five points allows the method to consistently identify up to two outliers while preserving enough inliers to fit the local model reliably. Further increasing the window would violate the assumption of approximate linearity within the window. The mass shifts in (i) are not selected randomly, every possible combination of two mass shifts out of five is selected because there are only
C
2
5
=
10
possible combinations. Consequently, the procedure is deterministic. As the window slides over all detected mass shifts, every mass shift receives an inlier or outlier vote each time it is part of the sliding window. Outliers are those mass shifts that receive more outlier votes than inlier votes and are ultimately discarded. The collection of accepted knots are expanded by knots at the boundaries of the m/z array and used for the initial estimate of the warping function. The addition of knots at the boundaries improves the control of the warping function in proximity to the boundaries, eliminating the need for extrapolation.
Once an initial estimate of the knots is obtained, it can be optimized by solving the optimization problem (see Figure
2D
). At this point, the assumption is made that the initial estimate is close to the global optimum; hence, the search space can be considerably reduced by opting for a small
Δ
value. L‐BFGS‐B [
19
] is used to solve the optimization problem. It is a quasi‐Newton method that updates an approximation of the inverse of the Hessian at every step and can handle simple box constraints on the input variables. It is empirically observed that the initial estimate considerably corrects the mass shift across the sample in most cases and that solving the optimization problem is time‐consuming. Therefore, performance metrics are also reported without solving the corresponding optimization problem for every spectra.
2.3
Evaluation Metrics
Although ground truth with respect to mass alignment is generally unavailable, the performance of an alignment procedure can be estimated by examining the mass dispersion of the peaks and the similarity of the mass spectra to the average mass spectrum before and after alignment. To compute the mass dispersion of the data, the average mass spectrum is used to detect the most intense peaks. The parabolic centroiding algorithm [
20
] is employed to obtain an estimate of the corresponding peak mass. Then, for every mass spectrum in the sample, peaks are identified within a window around the peak mass of width two times the peaks' full width at half‐maximum. The detected peak closest to the peak mass is chosen, and the standard deviation of the peak mass dispersion is computed.
A comprehensive evaluation of the methods requires the use of multiple metrics, as mass dispersion alone is insufficient to determine whether peaks originate from the same compound. While previous studies have primarily relied on mass dispersion to assess alignment quality, this work extends the evaluation by incorporating a similarity metric. This similarity metric provides stronger evidence for the correct correspondence of peaks. As described earlier, the cosine similarity is the chosen similarity metric.

3
Materials
The developed method is evaluated through its application to a large dataset. The dataset is generated from stage IV primary human glioblastoma multiforme sections with a RapifleX MALDI Tissuetyper TOF mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics) in negative ionization mode [
21
]. Specifically, the dataset includes 24 samples drawn from the larger cohort analyzed by Hendriks et al. [
21
]. Furthermore, REIMS measurements were generated from the remaining tissue using an electrical surgical knife [
22
] connected to a Xevo G2‐XS quadrupole time‐of‐flight mass spectrometer with a REIMS interface (Waters Corporation). Multiple incisions were made per sample. All patients (>11 years of age) were scheduled to undergo an elective neurosurgical procedure under total intravenous general anaesthesia. This single‐centre, prospective observational study was performed at Leuven University hospitals, Gasthuisberg (Leuven, Belgium). The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee Research UZ/KU Leuven (S60291) and the project was registered under the UZ Leuven Tissue Bank. The m/z range considered in this paper is 100–1000 Da. Each sample in the MALDI‐MSI dataset contains, on average, 45 313 spectra, with approximately 35 722 m/z values recorded per pixel. The complete dataset occupies a total of 186 GB of storage. More detailed information can be found in the supplementary information in Table
S1
. No additional preprocessing was performed on the dataset.
After reducing the intrasample misalignment of the MALDI images, the average MALDI mass spectrum can be aligned to the average REIMS measurement of the sample. This demonstrates the robustness of the developed approach.

1
Introduction
Mass spectrometry is an analytical technique used to measure the quantity of ionized molecules in a sample [
1
]. This technique results in a mass spectrum consisting of the ion count per mass‐to‐charge (m/z) ratio. Mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) quantifies mass spectra in a spatially resolved and systematic manner [
2
]. The resulting high‐dimensional image is a rich source of spatial and chemical information. The high mass spectral resolution is essential for correctly identifying compounds present in the sample. However, the measured mass spectra have empirically been observed to suffer from a shift in m/z values across the sample. This shift is typically more prevalent for instruments containing time‐of‐flight (TOF) detectors but has also been observed for other instruments [
3
]. Mass misalignment can occur because of a multitude of reasons in TOF instruments; for instance, thermal distortion of the TOF tube [
4
], contamination of the ion source [
5
], inhomogeneous matrix deposition [
6
], topography of the tissue and variations in sample thickness [
6
,
7
] can contribute to the mass shift phenomenon. This phenomenon can be addressed at the point of measurement, or afterwards through data‐driven correction methods. In this work, the former is referred to as
mass calibration
and the latter as
mass alignment
. Furthermore, it is important to differentiate between
relative mass alignment
and
absolute mass alignment
. The former is indicative of the consistency with which peaks are aligned, whereas the latter is a measure of the deviation between the measured and theoretical peak masses.
To resolve misalignment, mass calibration can be performed via internal and external mass calibration [
1
]. During internal mass calibration, a calibration compound can be introduced to a second inlet of the mass spectrometer, or the compound can be mixed with the analyte prior to analysis. This could potentially modify the analyte; hence, the former is preferred. During external mass calibration, a calibration compound with a known mass spectrum is fed to the mass spectrometer. Now, the mass spectrum is calibrated by determining a warping function from the measured spectrum and the calibration peaks. The warping function maps measured m/z values to those of the calibration peaks. Figure
1
depicts a toy example of such a warping function. This warping function is applied to all subsequent measurements. Hence, this calibration technique is unable to correct for mass shifts that arise due to changing conditions during the experiment. Gobom et al. [
8
] observed the mass shift phenomenon after external calibration and noted that the mass shift changes over time. Therefore, internal mass calibration obtains more accurate calibration results. However, the application of the calibration compound across the tissue sample in MSI could have undesirable ion suppression effects. Thus, internal calibration is not ubiquitous in an MSI setting [
9
].
FIGURE 1
A toy example of a warping function: (top) a mass spectrum with mass misalignment with respect to the reference mass spectrum; (middle) the warping function, which alters the m/z values corresponding to the mass spectrum to align, such that alignment between the spectra improves; (bottom) aligned mass spectra after warping the mass spectrum.
1.1
Mass Alignment
Computational mass alignment approaches warp all spectra to a common reference spectrum, which can be constructed using known compounds in the sample or, for instance, the average mass spectra of a mass spectrometry image. These data‐driven alignment approaches typically reduce the dimensionality of the problem by performing peak picking and subsequently matching the peaks. Later, the spurious matches are identified and removed before the final warping function is computed. This paper proposes an alternative method that does not discard the shapes of the peaks or parts of the signal with lower intensity and is therefore able to reliably correct large mass shifts.
Most existing algorithms perform peak matching by extracting peaks from the profile data, identifying peaks in the neighborhood of a given peak and considering the peaks matched if the m/z difference between the peaks is below a predefined threshold [
5
,
9
,
10
,
11
,
12
,
13
]. These algorithms differ in the manner spurious matches are identified and in the manner the final warping is computed. Böcker and Mäkinen [
10
] proposed several methods for the detection of spurious matches; all of these compute a linear function to map between peaks using a combinatorial algorithm robust to outliers. Spurious matches are eliminated based on the distance to the linear function and the final warping is computed by fitting a polynomial function (up to order 2) to the true matches. Kulkarni et al. [
11
] expanded on this method by ordering the pixel pairs according to the similarity between their peaks. A reference spectrum is iteratively generated based on the pixel pair ordering.
Boskamp et al. [
9
] improve the alignment by exploiting the fact that tryptic peptides are observed to be clustered around equidistant masses across the m/z range. These peaks are matched with the mass spectra, resulting in a Kendrick mass defect map that encodes the difference between the measured masses and the nearest, exact peptide masses. A statistical analysis of the map provides local warping functions and the complete warping function is obtained by linearly interpolating the remaining m/z bins. The method is not universally applicable due to the dependence on the chemical noise background and yields erroneous results in spectra dominated by matrix peaks and located in off‐tissue areas. Recently, Denker et al. [
12
] proposed a neural network to improve the work of Boskamp et al. The proposed neural network maps the Kendrick mass defect map to a warping function. Hence, the efficacy of this method is contingent on the presence of the chemical noise background. Additionally, the proposed method only considers mass defects within the range of roughly 0.5 Da due to the circular definition of the Kendrick mass defect map.
Eriksson et al. [
5
] developed another label‐free approach, called MSIWarp, which represents the peaks in the mass spectra as Gaussians and eliminates false matches by performing a random sample consensus (RANSAC) procedure [
14
]. However, the approximation of peaks using Gaussian functions can lead to inaccuracies in the case of peak asymmetry, a characteristic frequently observed in proteomics and metabolomics studies [
15
]. This approach models the warping function as a piecewise linear function that maximizes a similarity metric, which is based on the overlap of the Gaussians between spectra. The warping function is computed with dynamic programming.
In the work of La Rocca et al. [
13
], a Gaussian kernel is used to estimate the probability density function of the mass errors. Subsequently, matches are discarded based on the distance to the maximum of the distribution and RANSAC regression is used because the matches are not necessarily outlier‐free.
An example of an intrasample alignment method for which peak picking is not required is the work of Ràfols et al. [
3
]. Here, an initial linear warping is performed based on the cross‐correlation of the upper and lower parts of the mass spectrum and the reference spectrum. Afterwards, nonlinear Loess smoothing is applied to predict the calibrated m/z axis based on the relationship between reference masses and the average spectrum. Although there is a nonlinear step, the intrasample nonlinear relationships are not corrected.
This paper proposes a novel, peak‐picking–free approach for computing optimal nonlinear warping functions in mass alignment. The method directly estimates a smooth cubic spline warping function that maximizes the similarity between a reference mass spectrum and a warped mass spectrum. By avoiding the potentially unreliable peak‐picking step [
16
], this approach preserves the complete spectral signal, thereby enhancing robustness to noise. The robustness of the method is demonstrated by aligning spectra exhibiting significant mass shifts and correcting the relative mass misalignment between spectra across different MS modalities: matrix‐assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI‐MSI), rapid evaporative ionization mass spectrometry (REIMS) and desorption electrospray ionization (DESI) MSI.

Optimization further improves the initial estimates of the knots by maximizing the cosine similarity, which is associated with a reduction of the median mass dispersion, except for samples A and Q. Solving the subsequent optimization problem can drastically lower the error and improve the results if the initial estimate is in the neighborhood of the optimal warping function. The performance of the proposed method with optimization is slightly better than the performance of MSIWarp, whereas our method without optimization is outperformed by MSIWarp. Although the performance metrics of our method without optimization are worse than the method with optimization and MSIWarp, the execution time is found to be significantly faster than these methods, while still achieving a considerable reduction in mass misalignment. The choice of reference spectrum can significantly impact alignment performance, particularly for heterogeneous tissues such as our glioblastoma multiforme sections [
21

Since the average is taken after TIC normalization, the obtained spectrum is generated from equal contributions from all the spectra present in the tissue. Hence, consistent peaks in parts of the tissue will be represented in the final spectrum. However, as the mass dispersion increases, the average spectrum becomes a less suitable reference, and an alternative should be chosen. This is the case for samples V, W and X; as reported in Table

It is already established that the proposed method without optimization is considerably faster than the other approaches considered. Furthermore, experiments suggest that the proposed method with optimization is roughly three to four times as fast as MSIWarp. The computational complexity of the method is linear with respect to the number of mass spectra present in the sample and the number of segments considered [

These samples were chosen based on their limited size and the severity of mass shifts observed: Sample K exhibits severe mass shifts, while the mass shifts of L are mild. Usually, the expected amount of mass shift is known and parameters (ii) and (iii) can be chosen accordingly, eliminating one degree of freedom. In the experiment, the parameters are chosen such that the mass shift considered for the determination of the local alignment is identical for samples K or L. This allows for the assessment of the impact of varying (ii): the window size around the maximum peak per segment. If severe mass shifts are present, the correct determination of the local mass shift is expected to be harder when the window size increases, because it is more likely that the local mass shift is not appropriate for peaks in proximity to the window boundaries. This expectation is confirmed by the results of the experiment for sample K with severe mass shifts. On the contrary, for sample L with mild mass shifts, this effect is negligible.
Experiments were also conducted with various numbers of segments in which the mass spectra are divided. Eventually, this results in the number of knots and the size of the optimization problem after an optional outlier detection step. Performance metrics usually improve as the number of segments increases, because an increase in knots means that the spline function can approximate more complex warping functions. Additionally, the segments become smaller and may only contain peaks that are not present in both the mass spectrum and the reference spectrum, resulting in more outlier knots. In the event that multiple outlier knots exist in close proximity, true knots might be removed. However, outlier detection proves to be beneficial if the number of segments is not exceedingly small or large. For example, applying outlier detection to a sample with severe mass shifts and five segments deteriorates the performance metrics since the local mass shifts are far from linear (see Figure
5
). Nevertheless, applying the algorithm with outlier detection to samples that exhibit minor mass shifts is inconsequential because erroneous matches are already eliminated by a good choice of (ii) and (iii). Furthermore, the execution time hardly increases if the number of segments increases and the optimization problem is not solved. Conversely, the execution time increases sublinearly with the number of knots if the optimization problem is solved, thanks to the efficient computation of the gradient mentioned in the previous section.
The performance of our algorithm without optimization is a strong indicator of the performance of the algorithm with optimization, because the performance metrics for the former are empirically observed to be a lower bound for the latter (see Figure
3
). Because of this, the proposed method without optimization can be used to perform parameter optimization on a subset of the data, significantly speeding up the parameter selection process.
4.3
Multimodal Mass Alignment
Aside from solving mass misalignment within a sample of a single modality, the proposed method can also align mass spectra from different MS modalities, provided that there is a sufficient amount of shared information between the modalities. In this section, our method is applied to align the corrected MALDI‐MSI and REIMS measurements by computing a single warping function from the average MALDI‐MSI mass spectrum to the average REIMS mass spectrum per sample. The developed method expects the m/z array of the moving spectrum and the reference spectrum to be identical. Consequently, the REIMS measurements are binned to the m/z array of the MALDI‐TOF measurements since the REIMS data has a higher spectral resolution.
As the lower part of the m/z range is dominated by matrix‐related peaks that are not shared between the modalities, cross‐modal alignment is performed on the 600–900 Da m/z range. The distribution of the resulting cosine similarity before and after alignment is shown in Figure
7
. The average similarity improves from 0.101 to 0.180 after alignment using the initial estimates as knots for the warping function and to 0.189 after optimizing the knots. The cosine similarity between the mass spectra of MALDI‐MSI and REIMS roughly doubles after alignment. The relatively low cosine similarity values suggest that the amount of shared information is limited. Abundant peaks in one modality may not be present in the other, and the shapes of the peaks may differ between the modalities. Notwithstanding, the proposed methodology can considerably improve the metric.

4.4
Intersample Mass Alignment
Naturally, it is also possible to align the measurements across the samples. The average REIMS measurement across the tissues is used as a reference spectrum. After alignment of the REIMS measurements, the median mass dispersion of the 50 largest peaks improves from 12.15 to 6.70 ppm without optimization and to 6.08 ppm with optimization. Similarly, the MALDI‐MSI misalignment between samples can be reduced by computing a warping function from the average mass spectra of the samples to a reference spectrum, which can be chosen as the average mass spectrum of any sample. Then, the median mass dispersion of the 100 largest peaks of these average mass spectra improves from 105.10 to 23.60 ppm without optimization and to 19.48 ppm with optimization. Finally, the resulting average MALDI‐MSI mass spectra can be aligned with the resulting average REIMS mass spectra. This indirect approach to perform multimodal mass alignment improves the average similarity from 0.054 to 0.178 without optimization and to 0.181 with optimization.
4.5
General Applicability to Spectral Data
The main drawback of the proposed alignment approach with respect to applicability is the requirement of profile data. Consequently, the method is not applicable to centroided datasets. In the case of sparse mass spectrometry data, the algorithm can be applied after careful construction of a shared m/z array, as described in Section
2.2
.
To ensure the robustness of the algorithm, it is applied to two public datasets. The first dataset is generated from human cancer spheroids with a rapifleX MALDI TOF/TOF instrument (Bruker Daltonics) [
26
], and the second from a colorectal adenocarcinoma sample using a motorized DESI ion source and an LTQ XL Orbitrap Discovery instrument (Thermo Fischer Scientific) [
27
]. The first dataset is stored using a common m/z axis shared across all pixels, whereas the second dataset is stored in a sparse, centroided format with an individual m/z array for each pixel. After careful construction of a common m/z array, it is possible to apply our algorithm. Afterwards, it is possible to apply the computed warping functions to the separate m/z arrays individually.
For the spheroids dataset, our algorithm reduces the median mass dispersion from 19.02 to 11.12 ppm without optimization and to 10.54 ppm with optimization, whereas MSIWarp reduces it to 12.22 ppm. The cosine similarity improves from 0.6532 to 0.7972 without optimization, to 0.8079 with optimization and to 0.7941 with MSIWarp. Because of the limited number of peaks present in the spectra, MSIWarp is substantially faster for this dataset, taking only 1.48 s opposed to our algorithm, which requires 4.92 s without optimization and 81.38 s with optimization for 1201 mass spectra with 171 167 m/z bins and 23 peaks on average.
For the Orbitrap dataset, our algorithm executes in 8.39 s without optimization and in 291.09 s with optimization, whereas MSIWarp needs 358.16 s for 18 270 mass spectra with 16 569 m/z bins and 730 peaks on average. The median mass dispersion changes from 0.65 to 0.67 ppm without optimization, to 0.33 ppm with optimization and to 0.34 ppm with MSIWarp. Note that without optimization, the alignment does not improve for this instrument with high mass accuracy. This occurs because mass shifts exceeding the m/z bin width are rare for these instruments. Hence, an additional option is provided in these cases to optimize the knots starting from zero mass shifts. For completeness, the cosine similarity after alignment remains unchanged for our algorithm without optimization and improves from 0.9103 to 0.9130 with optimization and to 0.9127 with MSIWarp.
Furthermore, the proposed methodology is applicable to any modality that can benefit from alignment assuming that an initial estimate close to the optimal warping function can be determined reliably. To illustrate this general applicability, the method can be applied to spectral data with a limited number of peaks. For example, the proposed method is able to align 1D nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) metabolome profiles of table wines [
28
]. CluPA [
29
] is a method introduced specifically to align NMR data and improves the mean cosine similarity of the spectra with the average spectrum from 0.8486 to 0.9945, whereas the proposed algorithm without optimization improves the metric to 0.9946 and with optimization to 0.9968. This shows the general applicability of the proposed algorithm.
4.6
Implementation Details
The described algorithm is implemented in Python using Numba [
30
] to improve its execution speed. The optimization algorithm L‐BFGS‐B is implemented using SciPy [
31
]. Because the proposed algorithm warps every pixel independently, this is done in parallel. The experiments were performed on a laptop with an AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 7840HS CPU (3.8 GHz) that contains 8 cores and 32 GB RAM. The source code is available on GitHub:

Conclusions
This work proposes a fast and robust data‐driven algorithm to reduce the relative mass misalignment between mass spectra. First, a coarse alignment is computed based on the profile data and subsequently refined by solving a mathematical optimization problem to maximize the similarity between the mass spectra. The procedure does not require peak picking: The subtle features of profile spectra, such as the peak shape, contribute to the robust determination of the warping function. The proposed methodology is evaluated by performing extensive experiments on MALDI‐TOF MSI, REIMS and DESI‐Orbitrap MSI datasets and the performance metrics indicate that the refined alignment performs slightly better than MSIWarp, while the efficient coarse and refined alignment procedures reliably correct extreme mass shifts. The developed approach can perform intrasample, intersample and multimodal alignment, further demonstrating its robustness. Furthermore, the proposed methodology is shown to be generally applicable to any spectral data modality that exhibits sufficiently distinct spectral regions. By ensuring consistent mass alignment across mass spectra, our method enhances the integrity of downstream data analysis, which is especially important when working directly with profile data that retains subtle but informative spectral features.
A potential improvement involves the development of a framework that integrates our algorithm with a method that improves absolute mass alignment. The absolute mass accuracy can be improved either by calibrating the reference spectrum prior to alignment, or by refining the mass spectra following relative mass alignment.
